title: Ephesians 6
description: Ephesians 6 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 Children, listen to your parents in connection witha the lord since this is part of justness. 2 “Value your father and your mother.”b That’s the first direction with a promise, 3 “that it may goc well for you and you will be in the land a long time.”d 4 Fathers, do not be the cause of your children’s anger;e instead, nurturef them with childrearingg and directing their attention toh the Lord.

5 Enslaved workers, listen with openness of your heart to those who are lords based on bodily considerations,i with seriousness and trembling,j as in connection with Christ. 6 Do so not only while your work is being watched,k as people-pleasers, but as workers enslaved to Christ, doing what God desires from your very being, 7 serving with goodwilll as for the Lord and not for people 8 since you understand that each person who does what is beneficial—that person will be provided for by the Lord, whether enslaved or free. 9 Lords, you also do these things for them, giving up the use of threats, since you understand that the Lord in the heavens is both theirs and yours, and there is no discriminationm with him.

10 Finally, be strengthened by the Lord and with the Lord’s intense strength.n11 Put on the battle gearo associated with Godp in order to be able to withstand against the False Accuser’sq schemesr 12 because our battles is not against blood and bodyt but against the leaders, against the authorities, against the conquerors of the world systemu—who are characterized by this darknessv —and against the things that are associated with the oppressive spirit-breath in the highest heavens.w13 Because of this, wear the battle gear associated with God so that you can be able to stand up tox them on the day of oppression,y having accomplished everything necessary to take your stand.z 14 Therefore, take your standaa while binding your waistbb with truth and putting on the breastplate, justice, 15 and while binding readiness produced by the triumphant message of peace under your feet, 16 and while wearing with all of it the shield, faithfulness,cc with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of oppression.dd 17 Take in your hand the helmet, liberation,ee and the shortsword, the Life-breath, which comes from the mouthff of God. 18  Do so with every prayer and wholehearted request, praying in every moment with the Life-breath, and give it attention with persistence and a wholehearted request about all the sacred ones 19 and on my behalf, that what to say may be given to me when I open my mouth, along with courage to speak upgg and make known the mystery of the triumphant message— 20 which is why I am an ambassadorhh in chains—that I may have courage to speak as it is necessary to speak about it.

21 Tychicus, the beloved member of the Family and faithful servant with the lord, will make known everything to you so that you can understand everything about me and what I am doing 22 as I sent him to you for this very thing, that you may know about us and he may encourage your hearts.ii
23 To the members of the Family, peace and love with faithfulness from Father God and Lord Jesus Christ. 24 May good fortune be with all who undyinglyjj love our lord, Jesus Christ.

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘in,’ but that is only an appropriate translation for en if it is about location or time. It seems to be used here to indicate an unspecified connection ‘with reference to/with regard to’ and the basic idea seems to be that having a connection with the Lord leads logically to listening to parents, though it does not describe how that logic works explicitly.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: Citation of Exodus 20:12 and Deuteronomy 5:16

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: As in ‘happen’ or ‘come to pass’

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Citation of Deuteronomy 5:16

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Compare to Ephesians 4:26. It has the noun parorgismos (the cause of one’s anger), and this is the verb parorgizo (to cause anger).

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: This is the same word as in Ephesians 5:29 referring to caring for the needs of one’s body.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: This is paideia. Very literally, it is the practice of ‘childing.’ It refers to all the ways parents help their children learn and grow as people.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘instruction of.’ It’s a compound word for ‘mind’ and ‘attention.’ In other places, the traditional translation has to do with rebuke, but that is because the translators assume that calling someone’s attention to something necessarily means correcting them. As it is used in this verse, it seems to have a possible proactive use, not only reactive.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘according-to-the-flesh/body lords.’ What these ‘lords’ are basing their lordship on is shown to be a different priority than Christ’s priority. The word sarx (traditionally ‘flesh’) is not inherently bad or the opposite of godly. It literally means the stuff a body is comprised of. It can be used metaphorically or symbolically in a number of ways. One of those ways is to refer to ‘flesh and blood,’ meaning people of the same family. Family lineage has been a common way throughout history and cultures to determine who is owed allegiance and authority. It also has to do with the physical body, both in its drives and stature, so that people with ambition and strength and the impulse toward force and aggression both claim and are awarded privilege and power.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: Traditionally, “with fear and trembling.” The doubled phrase here is phobos kai tromos. Phobos covers a wide range of meanings in Greek, including terror, awe, reverence, serious regard, consequential recognition, and the English word ‘fear’ carries connotations (cowering, subordination, threat-response) that fit some but not all of the Pauline uses. This phrase occurs four other times in the New Testament: 1 Corinthians 2:3, where Paul describes his own posture coming to the Corinthians to plant the church (“I came to you in weakness and in fear and in much trembling”); 2 Corinthians 7:15, where it describes the Corinthians’ reception of Titus during a period of relational rupture and reconciliation; Philippians 2:12, where Paul encourages the community to “work out your own liberation with fear and trembling”; and Mark 16:8, where trembling paired with astonishment grips the women fleeing the empty tomb. In none of these contexts does the phrase describe a subordinate offering reverence or deference toward a superior. Paul is not subordinate to the Corinthians; the Corinthians are not subordinate to Titus; members of the Christ community working out their liberation are not being told to cower before God; the women at the tomb are beneficiaries of the resurrection, not subjects of a threatening power. The phrase names something else: the combination of cognitive recognition that stakes are high (phobos / seriousness) and the body’s registration of pressing through anxiety (tromos / trembling). Across the five uses, the person experiencing the phobos kai tromos is experiencing something consequential while aware of its weight. Here, “seriousness and trembling” names what is actually happening in enslaved labor under a potentially dangerous enslaver: the worker recognizes the real stakes, the body registers the real anxiety, and the work is done anyway as cruciform service to Christ (see verses 6–7). The passage does not ask enslaved workers to feel dignified about enslavement or to approach the enslaver with reverence. It names the actual conditions of the circumstance and encourages them to live cruciform lives because they are Christ’s followers, not because the enslavers own their loyalty.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘not according to eye-service.’

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: This word is a compound of ‘good/well’ and ‘mind.’ It only occurs here as a noun and in Matthew 5:25 (‘establish goodwill’) as a verb.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘favoritism’ or ‘partiality.’ There is a strong implication of not giving preference for those with high status against those with low status, not just ‘he has no favorites.’

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: This are the same Greek words found in Ephesians 1:19.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘panoply’ from panoplia. It means a ‘complete suit of armor.’

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: Probably in contrast to Caesar’s armor, the gear worn by Roman soldiers.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: The False Accuser was also mentioned in Ephesians 4:27.

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: The same word was used in Ephesians 4:14.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: This word, pale, refers specifically to a wrestling contest that was one by pinning the opponent with one’s hand to their throat.

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: Or ‘flesh and blood,’ including both the sense of ‘body’ and ‘family’ as part of what ‘flesh’ could symbolize.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: ‘The conquerors of the world’ is a single word in Greek, and it appears only here in the Bible. It is a compound of ‘world’ and a word that means something like ‘ruler’ but has as its root the meaning of seizing or obtaining by force.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: ‘This darkness’ refers to the darkness spoken of in Ephesians 5:7-11.

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘in the heavenlies.’ Literally, ‘in the over-sky’ or that which is higher than the sky. This has nothing to do with a post-death residence. It represents the level of authority or power of those who are said to be in this place. It represents socio-economic or power/authority status. In most places, God and Christ are said to be in this place, but here it points to oppressive forces also possessing that status.

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: Or ‘resist,’ but not in the sense of ‘exercise self-restraint.’ Rather, it’s in the sense of pushing back, taking a stand against injustice and oppressive forces.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘oppressive day’ or ‘harmful day.’ Traditionally, ‘evil day’ or ‘evil times.’

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘to stand.’

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘Therefore, stand’

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: ‘your’ is plural while ‘waist’ is singular.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: Or ‘trust.’ This is the Greek word pistis. In various places it can be translated as ‘trust,’ ‘faithfulness,’ or ‘allegiance.’ Traditionally, it is often translated as ‘faith’ or ‘belief (in).’ The clear sense is a trusting faithfulness or faithful trust. This trust and faithfulness is reciprocal and reinforces itself, the trust leading to a faithful response and faithfulness building trust, and the context is best served by highlighting one or the other more heavily. In this verse, it is difficult to say whether ‘trust’ or ‘faithfulness’ is more appropriate. I landed on ‘faithfulness’ only because Ephesians and Colossians seem both to lean more heavily on that usage overall, but it could make sense either way in this sentence. ‘Allegiance’ in the sense of the commitment to being faithful to a particular person (particularly a leader, such as Christ) or group or way of living/thinking is also sometimes the meaning of the word, and that could also work in this context.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: Or ‘the oppressor.’ Traditionally, ‘the evil one.’ See footnotes on ‘evil’ vs. ‘hardship’ or ‘oppression’ or ‘harm’ in Matthew 5.

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘salvation.’ It’s not incorrect, but it has become associated with ‘otherwordly’ connotations to be clear about what it is saying here. Other valid translations could be ‘salvation,’ ‘rescue,’ ‘preservation,’ ‘protection,’ ‘healing,’ ‘preventing/remediating harm.’

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘which is the word of God.’ This is from the Greek rema, not logos. It can mean ‘word’ but more literally means ‘utterance,’ meaning whatever is spoken or comes vocally from the mouth.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: Compare with Ephesians 3:12.

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Another possible translation for this word, though it does not seem to be relevant to the context, is ‘old man.’ Compare to Philemon 9.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: Since ‘heart’ did not represent all emotion but specifically desire or motivation, this phrase could be translated as something like ‘strengthen your motivation.’

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: Literally something like ‘who love our Lord, Jesus Christ, with undyingness.’
